subsystems.name: Low-frequency radio array
subsystems.role: catches the coherent radio emission that a planetary magnetic field should produce.

subsystems.name: Polarisation and dynamic-spectrum pipeline
subsystems.role: turns raw voltages into the signature of auroral emission.

subsystems.name: Interference and ionosphere mitigation
subsystems.role: removes the human and terrestrial noise that drowns faint planetary signals.

subsystems.name: Ultraviolet spectrograph
subsystems.role: measures hydrogen escaping the planet, an indirect probe of its magnetic shielding.

subsystems.name: Magnetosphere and bow-shock models
subsystems.role: predicts what the radio and UV signals should look like, and rules out other explanations.

subsystems.name: Stellar activity reference
subsystems.role: separates planetary signals from the star's own radio bursts and UV variability.

buildSteps.title: Pick hot, close planets
buildSteps.detail: Targets are gas giants on very short orbits, where the stellar wind is dense and the interaction should be strongest.

buildSteps.title: Estimate the emission frequency
buildSteps.detail: A planet's auroral radio emission should appear near its electron cyclotron frequency — roughly 2.8 MHz per gauss of polar field, tens of MHz for plausible hot-Jupiter fields — so the search band can be narrowed.

buildSteps.title: Observe across the whole orbit
buildSteps.detail: The array stares at the system for many hours, ideally covering a full orbital or rotation period, because the emission should be beamed and phase-modulated.

buildSteps.title: Strip the foreground
buildSteps.detail: Interference from aircraft, satellites and transmitters is flagged, and the ionosphere is calibrated out; only then is the residual examined.

buildSteps.title: Search for drifting polarised features
buildSteps.detail: The pipeline hunts narrowband, circularly polarised bursts that drift in frequency, and checks whether their timing matches the planet's orbit.

buildSteps.title: Measure the ultraviolet transit
buildSteps.detail: A space telescope watches the host star through a transit; extra absorption in the hydrogen Lyman-alpha line reveals gas escaping far beyond the planet's atmosphere.

buildSteps.title: Test the bow-shock picture
buildSteps.detail: Anomalously early absorption during ingress is compared with models of a magnetosphere standing off the stellar wind.

buildSteps.title: Confirm by consistency
buildSteps.detail: A claimed field must reproduce the radio period, the polarisation sense and the UV absorption depth together; stellar activity and instrumental artefacts are excluded before publication.

prerequisites.why: LOFAR and the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope already operate in the needed tens-of-MHz band; the Square Kilometre Array's low-frequency array is under construction and will be far more sensitive.
planetary emission is faint and sits among far stronger terrestrial signals.
Hubble remains the main facility capable of Lyman-alpha transit spectroscopy and is aging, so long campaigns are hard to schedule.
the geometry of a hot Jupiter's magnetosphere and how the wind drives aurorae are still actively debated.
without knowing the impinging wind, a measured field strength carries a large uncertainty.

pathway.milestone: searches on individual hot Jupiters with existing radio arrays, plus ultraviolet transit campaigns
pathway.unlocks: upper limits on magnetic fields and clear evidence that atmospheric escape is real, but no confirmed field detection.

pathway.milestone: a sensitive low-frequency array like SKA-Low surveying many systems
pathway.unlocks: enough targets to tell whether strong fields are common or rare.

pathway.milestone: simultaneous radio and ultraviolet observation of the same planet
pathway.unlocks: a field strength and an escape rate for one object, tying magnetism to atmosphere loss.

pathway.milestone: statistical surveys linked to stellar age and wind
pathway.unlocks: a way to judge which rocky planets can hold onto atmospheres long enough to matter.
